description: Structural and rhetorical patterns that mark machine-generated text. These are harder to detect than words because they live in the shape of the writing.

structures.name: Binary contrast
structures.pattern: "It's not X. It's Y." / "X is not Y. It is Z." / "Not X, but Y" / "X, not Y" / "That is not X. That is Y." / "That's not X. That is Y."
structures.example: The boom is priced on capex, not cash flow. The gap is not labor arbitrage. It is a trillion-parameter model. That is not hype. That is a procurement decision validated by real performance data.
structures.tell: AI reaches for the X-not-Y construction constantly because it produces the illusion of insight with zero content. It is the single most documented AI tell in detection studies. The declarative form ('X is not Y. It is Z.') is a contract-era tell on top of the classic negative-then-positive. The 'That is not X. That is Y.' variant is equally AI and must be caught.
structures.fix: State the positive alone. If the negation matters, split it into its own sentence and name the actor: 'Cash flow will decide who survives.'

structures.name: Trailing appended insight
structures.pattern: List or setup clause, then 'and [the real point]' tacked onto the end of the sentence
structures.example: The AI cost gap is architecture, subsidies, and strategy, and most buyers are reading the wrong number.
structures.tell: AI builds a sentence that appears complete, then appends the actual thesis after a final 'and' as if the point were an afterthought. Wire-style writers put the point first. The trailing-appendage version is a hallmark of LLM-generated business prose.
structures.fix: Promote the appended clause to its own sentence at the front: 'Most buyers are reading the wrong number. The gap is architecture, subsidies, and strategy.'

structures.name: Rule of three
structures.pattern: Three parallel items or adjectives
structures.example: Fast, reliable, and secure.
structures.tell: Human writers use it too, but AI uses it as a default rhythm in every paragraph. Three consecutive rule-of-three constructions is a strong tell.
structures.fix: Keep at most one per section. Vary sentence length deliberately.

structures.name: Uniform sentence length
structures.pattern: Every sentence roughly the same length
structures.example: The system tracks orders. It updates stock levels. It notifies customers.
structures.tell: LLM token prediction prefers similar-length sentences. Human writing has rhythmic variation: long, short, long.
structures.fix: Deliberately write one short sentence and one long sentence per paragraph.

structures.name: Hedging seesaw
structures.pattern: Claim + hedge + counterclaim + hedge
structures.example: AI will transform marketing. However, adoption varies. That said, early movers benefit.
structures.tell: AI balances every claim against its opposite to sound fair. The result is writing that never commits.
structures.fix: Commit to the claim, then name the real boundary condition once.

structures.name: Throat-clearing opener
structures.pattern: First paragraph says nothing, promises something
structures.example: In today's fast-paced world, businesses must adapt. In this article, we explore the key strategies that can help.
structures.tell: The first 1-2 sentences contain zero information. AI generates these as 'warm-up' tokens.
structures.fix: Open with a fact, a number, or a claim. Never open with a promise of content.

structures.name: Colon reveal
structures.pattern: Setup sentence + colon + payoff
structures.example: The answer is simpler than you think: consistency.
structures.tell: AI loves the colon setup because it delays the payoff for dramatic effect. Repeated colons are a tell.
structures.fix: Put the payoff first.

structures.name: Dramatic fragment
structures.pattern: Sentence fragment used for emphasis
structures.example: That's it. That's the whole thing.
structures.tell: AI fragments for dramatic rhythm. One is fine; a fragment in every paragraph is a tell.
structures.fix: Use fragments rarely and only where the drama is earned.

structures.name: Synonym cycling
structures.pattern: Repeating the same idea with different words to avoid repetition
structures.example: The agent handles your email. The assistant drafts replies. The copilot manages your inbox.
structures.tell: AI fears lexical repetition, so it cycles synonyms. Human writers repeat the same noun when it's the same thing.
structures.fix: Repeat the actual word. Repetition of the precise term reads human; synonym cycling reads AI.

structures.name: Superficial analysis
structures.pattern: Abstractions that name a quality without evidence
structures.example: Highlighting the team's commitment to innovation.
structures.tell: AI summarizes with abstract nouns instead of concrete actions. 'Commitment to innovation' carries no information.
structures.fix: Describe what was done. 'The team rewrote the parser twice to cut latency by 40%.'

structures.name: Importance puffery
structures.pattern: Claims of importance without evidence
structures.example: This marks a pivotal moment in the industry.
structures.tell: AI asserts significance instead of showing it. 'Pivotal', 'testament', 'marks a milestone' all belong here.
structures.fix: State the consequence. 'This changed the pricing model for every competitor within a quarter.'

structures.name: Fake-profound ending
structures.pattern: Closing line with cosmic significance, no content
structures.example: The future isn't coming. It's already here.
structures.tell: AI ends on a note that sounds meaningful but commits to nothing.
structures.fix: End with the decision, the number, or the next step.

structures.name: Weasel attribution
structures.pattern: Claims of consensus without sources
structures.example: Experts agree, studies show, research suggests, many believe.
structures.tell: AI fabricates authority by citing anonymous groups.
structures.fix: Name the source or drop the claim.

structures.name: Passive voice default
structures.pattern: Actions described without actors
structures.example: Mistakes were made. Decisions were taken. Improvements were implemented.
structures.tell: AI defaults to passive when unsure of the subject. Humans write active sentences because they know who did what.
structures.fix: Name the actor: 'We made mistakes. The board took the decision.'

structures.name: Corporate pep talk
structures.pattern: Motivational register in business text
structures.example: Together, we will unlock our full potential and drive value for all stakeholders.
structures.tell: AI generates the speech register when asked for 'professional' tone.
structures.fix: Write the sentence a smart colleague would actually say.

structures.name: Faux-inquiry setup
structures.pattern: Rhetorical question before the answer
structures.example: So, what does this mean for you? It means you need to act now.
structures.tell: AI uses the question-answer pair to simulate dialogue.
structures.fix: Answer directly. Let the reader ask the question.

structures.name: Enumeration overkill
structures.pattern: Every point numbered or bulleted
structures.example: 1. First... 2. Second... 3. Third...
structures.tell: AI structures everything as a list because it reduces generation risk. Prose needs variety.
structures.fix: Write in paragraphs; reserve lists for true enumerations.

structures.name: Anaphora stacking
structures.pattern: Repeated sentence-initial words
structures.example: We build. We ship. We iterate.
structures.tell: AI loves anaphora (repeated openers) for rhythm. Two or more in a row is a tell.
structures.fix: Vary the openers.

structures.name: Transition overdose
structures.pattern: A connective at the start of most sentences
structures.example: However... Additionally... Moreover... Finally...
structures.tell: AI cannot stop connecting sentences explicitly. Humans let sentences stand alone.
structures.fix: Delete most transitions. Let the content imply the relation.

structures.name: Jargon pile-up
structures.pattern: Three or more buzzwords in one sentence
structures.example: Leveraging synergistic ecosystems to drive holistic digital transformation.
structures.tell: AI responds to 'professional' prompts with buzzword soup.
structures.fix: Translate to plain language. If you cannot translate it, you don't know what it means.

structures.name: Emoji as structure
structures.pattern: Emoji used as bullet points or section dividers
structures.example:
✅ Fast setup
🚀 Scale on demand
🔒 Enterprise security
structures.tell: AI uses emoji bullets to make bland content look organized.
structures.fix: Use real bullets or real sections. Emoji only for actual status meaning.

structures.name: Hashtag stacks
structures.pattern: Five or more hashtags at the end of a post
structures.example: #innovation #growth #marketing #AI #future
structures.tell: AI generates hashtag clouds. Humans pick 2-3 specific ones.
structures.fix: Cut to 2-3 hashtags that name the actual audience.

structures.name: Markdown in plain text
structures.pattern: Asterisks or markdown syntax visible in a chat or email
structures.example: **This is important** and so is *this*.
structures.tell: AI composes in markdown and forgets to render it.
structures.fix: Render the formatting or strip the markers.

structures.name: Invented precision
structures.pattern: Statistics and quotes that do not exist
structures.example: Studies show 87% of teams report higher morale.
structures.tell: AI fabricates plausible numbers. The confidence is the tell.
structures.fix: Never include a number you cannot source. Write 'some teams' or find the real data.

structures.name: Universal sweep
structures.pattern: Claims that apply to everyone
structures.example: Every business needs this. No one can afford to ignore it.
structures.tell: AI generalizes because it lacks your specific context.
structures.fix: Name the specific segment: 'Teams with 10-200 employees and no ops layer.'

structures.name: Exclamation escalation
structures.pattern: More exclamation marks than the content earns
structures.example: This is amazing!! You won't believe it!!!
structures.tell: AI amps energy synthetically when asked for enthusiasm.
structures.fix: Write the energy with facts, not punctuation.

structures.name: Ellipsis trail
structures.pattern: Ending thoughts with ... to sound contemplative
structures.example: The answer, it turns out, is simpler than we thought...
structures.tell: AI uses the trailing ellipsis to fake human hesitation.
structures.fix: End the sentence with a period.

structures.name: Em dash sprinkle
structures.pattern: Em dashes (the long dash, written as -- in this dataset) as the default parenthesis
structures.example: The system -- which runs in production -- handles every request.
structures.tell: AI overuses em dashes because they are the easiest way to insert an aside. Multiple per paragraph is a tell.
structures.fix: Replace most em dashes with commas, parentheses, or separate sentences.

structures.name: Single-sentence-per-line fragmentation
structures.pattern: Every sentence rendered as its own standalone paragraph, with no grouped mini-paragraphs
structures.example:
Cursor was the best coding tool.

Anthropic and OpenAI own the stack.

Cursor rented brainpower.

Colossus fixes that.
structures.tell: This is the LinkedIn formatting trap: line-broken sentences masquerading as rhythm. High-signal founders write with varied cadence - a short punchy statement, then a standard two-to-three-sentence paragraph, then a single beat. Every-line-its-own-paragraph reads as either machine output or a content template. Detection requires comparing sentence count to paragraph count in the post body.
structures.fix: Group related sentences into two-to-three-sentence mini-paragraphs. Mix one short standalone line with one standard paragraph per section. A post of fifteen lines should compress to six-to-eight visible paragraphs.

structures.name: Litotes (negation hedging)
structures.pattern: Understatement through double negative or negated opposite: 'not uncommon', 'not insignificant', 'not without merit', 'far from trivial', 'by no means'
structures.example: The results are not insignificant. It is not uncommon for teams to underperform in this area. The challenge is far from trivial.
structures.tell: AI reaches for litotes to sound measured while committing to nothing. Instead of saying 'the results matter' or 'teams often underperform', it wraps the claim in a double negative that hedges through understatement. Humans who mean something say it. 'Not uncommon' means 'common' but sounds less committal. This is distinct from binary contrast (which sets up X vs Y): litotes negates the opposite of what it means, producing a sentence that is technically true but semantically evasive. One instance is a style choice; two or more in a passage is a hedge pattern.
structures.fix: State the positive directly. 'Not insignificant' becomes 'significant'. 'Not uncommon' becomes 'common' or 'frequent'. 'Far from trivial' becomes 'hard' or name the specific difficulty. 'By no means' becomes a direct assertion or a specific constraint.

structures.name: Hedging qualifier chains
structures.pattern: Three or more hedges stacked in a single sentence: 'might potentially possibly', 'could potentially help in certain contexts', 'may potentially represent a meaningful shift'
structures.example: This approach might potentially help some teams improve productivity in certain contexts, though results may vary depending on various factors.
structures.tell: AI stacks qualifiers because each hedge reduces the probability of being wrong. Three hedges in one sentence produce a claim so diluted it carries no information. The reader finishes the sentence unable to determine whether the writer believes the claim or not. One hedge is careful writing. Three is evasion.
structures.fix: Commit to the claim or drop it. If you believe it, say it. If you're unsure, name the specific condition that decides it: 'This works for teams under ten. Past that, the standup format collapses.'

structures.name: Restating the question as the answer
structures.pattern: A question is asked, and the 'answer' explains why the question matters instead of providing an answer
structures.example: How much does it cost? Pricing is an important consideration when choosing any tool. Costs can vary based on your needs, usage, and the features you require.
structures.tell: AI generates answer-shaped text that contains zero actual information. The response restates the question in declarative form, adds context about why the question is important, and finishes without ever naming a number, a range, or a decision criterion. This is especially common in FAQ sections and answer-box content.
structures.fix: Answer the question in the first sentence. 'It costs $12/month billed annually, or $18 month-to-month.' If you cannot name a specific number, name the factors that decide it and give a range.

structures.name: Listicle filler
structures.pattern: Bullet points or numbered items that restate the heading in different words without adding information
structures.example: Benefits of drinking water: 1) Hydration is essential for your body. 2) Staying hydrated supports overall wellness. 3) Water helps maintain your body's hydration levels.
structures.tell: AI generates list items that are grammatically distinct but informationally identical. Each bullet rephrases the same empty claim. A human who knows the topic adds a new fact per bullet. AI adds a new sentence per bullet.
structures.fix: Each list item must add one concrete fact the reader did not have before. If you cannot write a distinct fact for each item, write fewer items.

structures.name: Staccato sentence stacking
structures.pattern: Three or more short declarative sentences (under 12 words each) in a row within the same paragraph, connected only by periods
structures.example: NVIDIA hired Groq's founder. NVIDIA licensed Groq's technology. And now NVIDIA is investing in the company that remains.
structures.tell: AI defaults to short subject-verb-object sentences because they are statistically safe. Humans writing naturally connect related ideas with commas, conjunctions, and dependent clauses. Three or more consecutive short sentences with identical structure (especially repeating the same subject like 'NVIDIA') is a machine rhythm tell. Real analysis flows; it does not index-card.
structures.fix: Merge related sentences using commas, conjunctions (and, but, because, while), or dependent clauses. 'NVIDIA hired Groq's founder, licensed its technology, and is now investing in the shell that remains.' The reader should feel the ideas connecting, not stacked.

structures.name: Strawman contrast pivot
structures.pattern: "Everyone is focused on X. I keep thinking about Y." / "Everyone is talking about X. I'm thinking about Y." / "The headlines are about X. What I can't stop thinking about is Y." / "Everyone fixates on X. I keep coming back to Y."
structures.example: Everyone is focused on the valuation. I keep thinking about the listing route. Everyone is talking about the revenue. I keep coming back to the chip effort.
structures.tell: AI constructs a fake audience ('everyone') to set up a strawman, then pivots to the writer's supposedly deeper insight. The pattern always follows the same shape: what others think (wrong/superficial) vs what I think (deeper/real). Real writers state their insight directly without manufacturing a contrast against an imaginary consensus. The 'I keep thinking about' / 'I keep coming back to' phrasing is the AI's default first-person insertion for this pattern.
structures.fix: State your insight directly. 'The STAR Market listing choice matters more than the valuation number.' No need to first describe what everyone else is thinking.

structures.name: Parallel conditional stacking
structures.pattern: Two or more "If X, Y." sentences stacked back to back in the same paragraph
structures.example: If the chip effort stalls, the model story weakens. If back-half revenue slows, the valuation looks thin.
structures.tell: AI stacks parallel conditionals because each one is individually safe to generate. Two or more in a row creates a metronomic rhythm that reads as list-generation, not thinking. Real writers connect related conditions or pick the more important one.
structures.fix: Merge into one sentence: 'A chip stall or revenue slowdown would both strain the $74 billion valuation.' Or pick the more important condition and state it alone.

structures.name: Negative listing
structures.pattern: "Not a X. Not a Y. A Z." / "It wasn't X. It wasn't Y. It was Z."
structures.example: Not a tool. Not a platform. A movement.
structures.tell: Binary contrast's louder cousin: the rhetorical striptease builds runway by negating near-misses before revealing the thing. The reveal only feels big because of the runway, which is manufactured drama, not information.
structures.fix: State Z directly: 'A movement.' If the near-misses matter, make them a real comparison with criteria.

structures.name: False agency
structures.pattern: Inanimate things performing human actions: 'the data tells us', 'the decision emerges', 'the market rewards', 'the culture shifts', 'a complaint becomes a fix'
structures.example: The data tells us the market rewards speed, and the culture shifts toward shipping.
structures.tell: An LLM favorite because it avoids naming the actor. Data sits there until someone reads it; decisions do not emerge; markets do not reward, buyers pay. Every false-agency sentence hides a person who did something.
structures.fix: Name the human, or use 'you': 'Two analysts read the data and cut the review to one day.'

structures.name: Self-answered question
structures.pattern: "Does this work? Absolutely." / "Is it worth it? Unquestionably." / "Can you? Yes."
structures.example: Does the free tier convert? Absolutely.
structures.tell: A rhetorical question the text immediately answers with an adverb of certainty. The Q&A format simulates evidence while providing none; the answer carries no data, only agreement with itself.
structures.fix: Answer with the evidence, or cut the question: 'The free tier converts at 4.2%.'

structures.name: Micro-heading stacking
structures.pattern: A heading over one or two sentences, repeated down the page (LinkedIn and newsletter format)
structures.example:
## Why it matters
One line. ## What to do
One line. ## The bottom line
One line.
structures.tell: Formatting where prose should be. When every two-sentence unit needs its own heading, the headings are doing the emphasis the writing cannot. Common in AI-generated LinkedIn carousels and newsletter sections.
structures.fix: Merge the fragments into paragraphs with real transitions. Keep headings for sections of three or more paragraphs.

structures.name: Catalog dump
structures.pattern: A comma-separated inventory of nouns in one breath, with no analysis of any item
structures.example: Teams use it for sales, marketing, support, ops, finance, hiring, legal and product.
structures.tell: Breadth substituted for substance. The list reads as comprehensive while committing to nothing about any item on it; coverage phrasing in list form.
structures.fix: Cut to the two items you can say something specific about.
